extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and practitioners of stand-up comedy, and researchers of comedic style
extracted.subtask_description: Extract criteria and evaluative features for writing and performing stand-up comedy (as exemplified by Bill Hicks), focusing on material, delivery, audience relationship, and ethical/medium constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance as emotional play
rubrics_metrics.description: Hicks' performance style was seen as a play on his audience's emotions. He expressed anger, disgust, and apathy while addressing the audience in a casual and personal manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use emotional extremes (anger, disgust, apathy) deliberately to shape audience response while maintaining a casual, conversational delivery to create intimacy and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speak to the audience as friends / conversational tone
rubrics_metrics.description: He likened addressing the audience to merely conversing with his friends and spoke 'as though they were his friends.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a conversational, personal manner rather than a distant lecturing tone; treat the audience as adults and equals to foster engagement and trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invite audiences to challenge authority and accepted truths
rubrics_metrics.description: He would invite his audiences to challenge authority and the existential nature of 'accepted truth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft material that provokes thought and questions commonly held beliefs; aim to unsettle complacency rather than only to amuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of stylistic devices (e.g., news-report parody)
rubrics_metrics.description: One message was delivered in the style of a news report (to draw attention to the negative slant news organizations give to any story about drugs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ recognizable formats (news report, mock interview, etc.) to refract and satirize real-world institutions or media practices; use the device to highlight bias or absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical and controversial subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: His material encompassed a wide range of social issues including religion, politics, and philosophy—was controversial and often steeped in dark comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tackle religion, politics, consumerism, drugs, and other charged topics if your intent is provocative satire; expect and accept controversy as part of the terrain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity / staying true to beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: When challenged about offending audiences, Hicks argued it was his show and that he should not change his own outlook and beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize authentic voice and convictions over pandering; audiences often respond to perceived sincerity even when offended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cheap shock tactics; aim for substantive provocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Jimmy Carr noted 'When Hicks got it right, when he resisted the cheap shock tactics and hit his evangelical peak, it was awesome...' implying cheap shock is an anti-pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use provocation that has intellectual or emotional payoff rather than mere shock for its own sake; cheap shocks risk being dismissed and not 'moving.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and ownership of material
rubrics_metrics.description: Denis Leary's album featured lines and subject matter similar to Hicks's routine; multiple comics have stated Leary stole Hicks's material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain clear authorship and originality; avoid copying others' lines/persona — plagiarism damages reputation and professional relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium suitability and censorship risk
rubrics_metrics.description: NBC had a policy that no jokes about handicapped people would be aired; Letterman removed Hicks's entire 1993 Late Show performance because producers believed the material was unsuitable for broadcast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that television and other mass media have content constraints; adapt material if you want it broadcast, or accept removal/censorship if you prioritize uncensored expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of recurring motifs and a signature closing
rubrics_metrics.description: He closed shows with his philosophy 'It's Just a Ride' and had recurring themes (e.g., smoking/nicotine addiction) that figured heavily in his performances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop recurring lines, themes, or a signature closing to build a recognizable comic identity and to give performances thematic cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a consistent persona (including provocative persona)
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of Hicks' routine involved direct attacks on mainstream society, religion, politics, and consumerism; at times he delivered misanthropic tirades as part of his act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a coherent stage persona (angry satirist, outsider prophet, etc.) that aligns with your material; inconsistency between persona and content weakens impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept audience alienation as a possible outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasionally audience members did not find his material funny but Hicks argued it was impossible to please everyone and not his responsibility to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and accept that provocative material will alienate some listeners; decide whether alienation is an acceptable trade-off for the intended message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ephemeral, dated references where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Stewart Lee said Hicks's 'first two albums have dated badly, with their adolescent potshots at inoffensive figures from popular culture.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor material and constructions that have lasting resonance rather than quick potshots at ephemeral targets to maintain longevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide and manage stance toward political correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Hicks was strongly against political correctness, joking that the politically correct should be 'hunted down and killed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about your stance toward political correctness as part of your voice, but be mindful of consequences — it shapes audience perception and potential backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground controversial material in intellectual or philosophical sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Terence McKenna was a frequent source of Hicks' most controversial psychedelic and philosophical counter-cultural material; he acted out McKenna's 'Stoned Ape' model in routines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use referenced ideas or intellectual frameworks to give depth to controversial claims; citing or dramatizing source material can lend credibility and texture to satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hone material through high-volume performance
rubrics_metrics.description: He performed about 300 times a year during a period, implying heavy stage time to develop craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refine jokes and delivery through frequent live performance; repetition and iteration are key to sharpening timing, response to hecklers, and overall polish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heckler management and escalation risks
rubrics_metrics.description: In a 1989 gig, after a heckler shouted 'Free Bird' Hicks screamed 'Hitler had the right idea...' and followed with an extreme misanthropic tirade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare strategies for heckler handling; while sharp put-downs can be effective, escalating to extreme or offensive rhetoric carries reputational risk and may overshadow the act.
